heroTitle: Make room for the week you actually have.
heroDescription: A few patterns from your answers, and one small experiment to explore.

persona.name: Sam
persona.goal: Build a routine that still fits when work gets busy, without waiting for a fresh week to restart.

answers.question: What would you like to change?
answers.text: I want a routine I can keep during busy weeks. I would like movement to feel like part of my week rather than another project to restart.

answers.question: What has happened with previous plans?
answers.text: I usually start with three 45-minute evening workouts. After two or three weeks, late meetings get in the way and I stop.

answers.question: What tends to disrupt your plans?
answers.text: My work hours change. A meeting can be added near the end of the day, so I cannot promise the same finish time.

answers.question: What happens after you miss a session?
answers.text: When I miss a session, I often decide I will start again properly on Monday.

answers.question: What already feels easier to begin?
answers.text: I enjoy a relaxed weekend walk. It is easy to start because I do not need equipment or a perfect time slot.

answers.question: Where might a smaller activity fit?
answers.text: On two mornings next week, I can probably find ten minutes before work. I have not tried using that time for a walk yet.

answers.question: What would you prefer to try first?
answers.text: For now, I would rather try a short walk I already feel comfortable doing than commit to a new gym plan.

answers.question: How would you prefer to reflect on the experiment?
answers.text: A quick note about what got in the way would be easier for me to keep than tracking lots of numbers.

sections.title: Your personal starting point
sections.body: You want a routine that still fits when work gets busy. Your previous plan asked for three 45-minute evenings each week; late meetings often interrupted it. For now, you would prefer a short, familiar walk over starting another gym plan.
bullets: What matters to you: a routine you can return to without waiting for a fresh week.

sections.title: What your answers reveal
sections.body: Three observations connect directly to what you described.
bullets: Your evening plans compete with changing work hours. You described late meetings interrupting the time you had set aside.
A missed session sometimes becomes a delayed restart. You said you often wait until Monday to begin again.
Low-preparation movement already feels easier to begin. Your weekend walk needs little setup, and you would like to try something similarly simple.

items.title: Changing work hours
items.text: Your evening plans compete with meetings that can be added at short notice.

items.title: A delayed restart
items.text: You often wait until Monday after a missed session.

items.title: An easier beginning
items.text: A familiar walk needs little preparation and already appeals to you.

sections.title: Why previous attempts may have been difficult
sections.body: Your plan depended on a clear 45-minute evening window, while your work could change at short notice. That mismatch may have made the plan difficult to repeat. Waiting until Monday after a missed session may also have extended the interruption. These are possible explanations from your answers. We have not established whether other factors also played a part.

sections.title: Your potential blind spots
sections.body: Could the size of the planned session be making it harder to return? You described both a 45-minute plan and a habit of restarting “properly.” It may be worth exploring whether a smaller version would still feel worthwhile to you.
bullets: A morning window is a possibility, not yet a pattern. You identified two likely ten-minute openings. Trying one would tell us more than assuming it will fit.

sections.title: What could work better for you
sections.body: Try planning two short, familiar walks in the morning windows you identified. Choose a backup window at the same time, so a disrupted day already has an alternative. Keep the question small: “Did this fit my real week?” A brief note about what helped or got in the way will be more useful for this experiment than a demanding tracking system.

sections.title: Your stepping stones
sections.body: Start with three small actions. Adjust the plan from what you learn.
bullets: Choose two openings. Pick the two mornings you expect to have ten minutes, plus one backup window.
Make starting simple. Choose a familiar route and put what you need by the door.
Leave one honest note. After each planned attempt, write what happened—even if the walk did not happen.

sections.title: Your personal if-then rules
sections.body: These are draft rules to try and refine, not statements about what you already do.
bullets: If a late meeting removes my planned evening time, then I will look at my next agreed backup window.
If I miss a planned walk, then I will note the obstacle and choose the next suitable opportunity instead of automatically waiting until Monday.
If a morning window proves unrealistic, then I will change the timing before making the activity longer.

sections.title: Your seven-day experiment
sections.body: One question: can two short, familiar walks fit around a changing work week? What counts as useful is an honest observation about whether the plan fits. This experiment does not promise a particular fitness result.
bullets: Day 1 — Choose. Select two likely ten-minute windows and one backup.
Days 2–3 — Try the first window. If it fits, take the familiar walk you chose. If it does not, note the obstacle and consider your backup.
Day 4 — Adjust one thing. Review your note. Keep or change the timing; do not add a more demanding plan.
Days 5–6 — Try the second window. Use what you learned from the first attempt.
Day 7 — Review. What did you try? What happened? What helped? What got in the way? What would you change next week?

sections.title: Open questions
sections.body: A useful report can leave questions open.
bullets: Will the two morning windows remain available in a busy week? We have not tested that yet.
Would a different backup time fit better than mornings?
What would make a short session feel worthwhile enough to repeat?
Are there other constraints you would want to discuss before choosing a routine?

sections.title: The next step with JZPT
sections.body: You can try this experiment on your own. If you would like to explore what fits your life with someone, a Transformation Blueprint session can build on these observations and help shape a realistic next step.
